## What SDID adds

Synthetic difference-in-differences (SDID) combines a weighted comparison group with a weighted before–after comparison. **Unit weights** make untreated units resemble the treated group's pre-treatment trajectory; **time weights** make selected pre-treatment periods more informative about the post-treatment comparison. A DiD calculation then removes the remaining weighted baseline gap [@arkhangelsky2021synthetic].

This gives SDID a useful place alongside [classical synthetic control](synthetic-control.qmd) and [difference-in-differences](../did/difference-in-differences.qmd). A treated place can have a persistently higher outcome level than its donors and still have a useful comparison trajectory. SDID accommodates that level difference explicitly. It still needs credible untreated comparisons and a defensible account of how outcomes would have evolved without treatment.

## Design and target

Start with a balanced panel: the same units are observed in every period. There are $N_0$ untreated donor units, $N_1$ treated units, $T_0$ pre-treatment periods, and $T_1$ post-treatment periods. Every treated unit begins treatment at the same boundary and remains treated. Donors remain untreated throughout.

The target is the average treatment effect across the treated unit–period observations:

$$
\tau_{ATT}=\frac{1}{N_1T_1}
\sum_{i\in\mathcal T}\sum_{t>T_0}
\{Y_{it}(1)-Y_{it}(0)\}.
$$

This is an average over the stated treatment window. It does not by itself describe the effect in each year, and changing the window changes the target. A single treated unit is permitted for point estimation, but creates special inference difficulties.

The baseline estimator and the standard `synthdid` interface use this **common-adoption block design**. Do not pass a staggered-adoption panel through the same setup and interpret the result as a general staggered DiD estimator. Cohort-specific designs and their aggregation require additional decisions about controls, exposure windows, and target weights. The paper discusses an extension; the [modern DiD notes](../did/callaway-santanna-multiple-periods-notes.qmd) provide a separate route for group-time effects.

## How the weights work

### Unit weights: match the trajectory up to a level shift

Choose non-negative donor weights $\widehat\omega_i$ that sum to one. They make the weighted donor outcomes track the treated group's average outcomes before treatment. The fitting problem includes an intercept and a regularisation penalty on the donor weights.

The intercept allows a persistent vertical difference between the two paths. The penalty discourages an excessively concentrated fit to noisy observations. Consequently, these are generally different weights from classical SCM, which seeks a match in levels without this intercept. SDID's ability to accommodate a level difference does not imply that it can repair arbitrary differences in trend.

### Time weights: learn a useful baseline from untreated units

Choose non-negative pre-treatment weights $\widehat\lambda_t$ that sum to one. Across the donor units, the weighted pre-treatment outcomes should predict average post-treatment outcomes up to an intercept. Each post-treatment period receives weight $1/T_1$ in the target average.

**Time weights use donors' post-treatment outcomes.** Those outcomes are untreated under the design. Treated post-treatment outcomes are reserved for measuring the effect, rather than selecting weights that produce a desired answer. This distinction is why the blanket instruction “learn every weight using only pre-treatment data” is inaccurate for SDID.

The paper regularises unit weights and adds only a very small regularisation term to make time weights unique in implementation. The two weighting problems are related, but their tuning is not interchangeable [@arkhangelsky2021synthetic, Section 2 of the July draft].

### Difference the weighted gaps

For each period, define the treated-minus-donor gap

$$
g_t=\frac{1}{N_1}\sum_{i\in\mathcal T}Y_{it}
-\sum_{i\in\mathcal C}\widehat\omega_iY_{it}.
$$

In the block design, the SDID estimate can be written as

$$
\widehat\tau_{SDID}
=\underbrace{\frac{1}{T_1}\sum_{t>T_0}g_t}_{\text{average post-treatment gap}}
-\underbrace{\sum_{t\leq T_0}\widehat\lambda_tg_t}_{\text{weighted pre-treatment gap}}.
$$

Equivalently, it is the treatment coefficient in a weighted least-squares regression with unit and time fixed effects, using the product of the unit and time weights. Treated units receive equal weight within the treated group. The weighted-gap expression makes clear what the fixed effects accomplish: a persistent baseline difference is subtracted before interpreting the remaining change as an effect.

## Worked example: why the baseline gap matters

Suppose the donor weights have already been estimated. The following invented outcomes illustrate the final calculation; the time weights are supplied for the exercise rather than fitted from these four rows.

| Period | Treated outcome | Weighted donor outcome | Gap $g_t$ | Weight within period group |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Pre 1 | 100 | 90 | 10 | 0.25 |
| Pre 2 | 108 | 94 | 14 | 0.75 |
| Post 1 | 111 | 103 | 8 | 0.50 |
| Post 2 | 113 | 107 | 6 | 0.50 |

The weighted baseline gap is $0.25(10)+0.75(14)=13$. The average post-treatment gap is $0.5(8)+0.5(6)=7$. Therefore,

$$\widehat\tau_{SDID}=7-13=-6.$$

The estimate is a reduction of six outcome units relative to the counterfactual, even though treated outcomes remain above donor outcomes. Using the raw post-treatment gap would instead report $+7$ and miss the baseline adjustment. Holding the donor weights fixed but using equal pre-period weights gives $7-12=-5$; this isolates the contribution of time weighting, rather than reproducing an unweighted DiD analysis.

**Check:** add 20 to the treated outcome in every period. Both gaps in the final subtraction rise by 20, so the estimated effect remains $-6$. This invariance to a constant level shift is central to the DiD part of SDID.

## Comparison with neighbouring methods

| Method | Main construction | Practical distinction |
|---|---|---|
| Ordinary DiD, common-adoption benchmark | Compare average changes between treated and untreated groups | Requires a credible parallel untreated trend for that comparison |
| Classical SCM | Match pre-treatment levels using a convex donor combination | Strong level fit is central; the usual post-treatment gap is not automatically baseline-adjusted |
| SDID | Learn donor and time weights, then difference weighted gaps | Allows a persistent level gap while seeking a more comparable change |
| Augmented SCM | Correct residual SCM imbalance using an outcome model | Ridge augmentation can imply negative donor weights; it is a different adjustment from SDID's time weighting and differencing |

These distinctions help choose a design; they do not establish a universal ranking. Compare [augmented SCM](augmented-synthetic-control-method-notes.qmd) for its bias-correction argument. Weighting can also cost precision when the unweighted groups are already suitable comparisons [@benmichael2021augmented; @arkhangelsky2021synthetic].

## What identification still requires

The paper analyses untreated outcomes with latent unit factors interacting with latent time factors. This allows richer patterns than a purely additive unit-and-time model. Its consistency results require conditions on balance, weight dispersion, panel size, and the noise process; they do not say that optimisation removes every source of confounding [@arkhangelsky2021synthetic, Section 4 of the July draft].

For an applied evaluation, investigate:

- **Anticipation and contamination:** treatment should not already affect the designated baseline, and donors must provide untreated outcomes throughout the comparison window.
- **Comparability over time:** pre-treatment similarity must be informative about the missing untreated path after treatment. A new treated-unit shock at the intervention date remains a rival explanation.
- **Support and concentration:** inspect which donors and baseline periods carry the estimate. A large nominal panel can still depend on one donor or one year.
- **Residual dynamics:** a constant level gap is accommodated; a persistent slope difference or unstable gap deserves investigation. Good fitted pre-treatment balance alone cannot prove identification.

The paper describes a form of robustness from balancing both the unit and time dimensions. Read this within its factor-model conditions, rather than as the claim that either a good-looking SCM plot or an ordinary parallel-trends test guarantees validity. For donor spillovers, consult [inclusive SCM](inclusive-synthetic-control-method-notes.qmd); baseline SDID does not itself estimate spillover effects.

## Inference: count treated units, not just observations

The paper develops three procedures [@arkhangelsky2021synthetic, Section 5 of the July draft]:

| Procedure | What it does | Important boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Unit bootstrap | Resamples whole unit histories and re-estimates SDID | Intended for settings with enough treated and control units; individual unit–period resampling loses within-unit dependence |
| Fixed-weight jackknife | Leaves out units while holding the estimated weights fixed | Not defined with one treated unit; its justification differs from simply re-fitting every component |
| Placebo variance | Assigns placebo treatment among controls and uses the dispersion of estimates | Can address a single treated unit, but requires comparability of the treated and donor noise processes, including the homoskedasticity condition used in the paper |

More years for one treated place do not create more independently treated places. A conventional regression standard error after fitting weights is not a substitute for an inference procedure justified for SDID and the actual design. Likewise, a placebo distribution is not automatically an exact randomisation test when policy assignment was not random.

## Applying the note

For a policy evaluation, first specify the treated units, common adoption date, outcome scale, donor exclusions, and post-treatment averaging window. Plot raw and weighted paths, report both sets of weights, and distinguish a tolerable level difference from a problematic changing gap. Re-estimate after defensible changes to donors or the baseline window, and report how the target or comparison changes.

The authors' R workflow uses `panel.matrices()` to construct the panel, `synthdid_estimate()` to estimate the effect, and `vcov()` with a supported method for inference. Their [worked software example](https://synth-inference.github.io/synthdid/) uses California Proposition 99 and placebo variance. This is an implementation reference; no new executed lab or numerical replication is supplied by this note [@synthdid-package].

For teaching, pair the weighted-gap exercise with the [California SCM source note](california-tobacco-synthetic-control-notes.qmd) and the [Proposition 99 lab](../../labs/synthetic-control-proposition-99-lab.qmd). Ask learners to identify which comparison changes when moving from SCM to SDID, rather than attributing every difference in estimates to a “better” method.
